decks.title: Aggregate Demand, Consumption and Saving — Part 1: Plans, Outcomes and Aggregate Demand
goals: Distinguish ex ante (planned) from ex post (realised) values and explain why realised saving equals realised investment
Explain the meaning of effective demand
List the components of aggregate demand and calculate it; express aggregate supply as consumption plus saving

slides.heading: Aggregate Demand, Consumption and Saving
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **planned** and **realised** values, **effective demand**, and the components of **aggregate demand** and **aggregate supply**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: aggregate demand, its components, aggregate supply, planned and realised values, how plans are reconciled, and effective demand
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: How much an economy produces depends on how much its people, firms, government and foreign buyers plan to spend. In this part we add up that planned spending as aggregate demand, compare it with the value of output, and see what happens when plans and outcomes differ.

slides.heading: Aggregate demand and its four parts
slides.body_md: **Aggregate demand** is the total **planned** spending on final goods and services in an economy during a period.

rows: A Jaipur family buys a mixer-grinder
A Pune factory installs a new press and adds to its stock
A state buys ambulances for district hospitals
Buyers abroad, less spending on foreign goods
Prawns sold to a hotel abroad, minus imported phones

visual.alt: Table of the four components of aggregate demand: private consumption by households, investment by firms, government expenditure, and net exports (exports minus imports), each with an imagined Indian example

slides.narration: Aggregate demand is everything that buyers plan to spend on the final output of an economy. Households buy consumer goods, firms buy machines and add to stocks, the government buys services and equipment, and foreigners buy our exports. Spending on imports goes to output made abroad, so it is taken away.

slides.heading: The aggregate demand formula
slides.body_md: In an open economy with a government: **AD = C + I + G + (X − M)**. In a simple two-sector economy: AD = C + I.

visual.alt: Flow building aggregate demand as consumption plus investment plus government expenditure plus exports minus imports
visual.caption: Adding up planned spending

slides.narration: Put the four parts together and you have the formula. Consumption, investment and government spending are added. Exports are added because foreigners buy our output. Imports are subtracted because that part of our spending buys output made elsewhere. With only households and firms, aggregate demand is simply consumption plus investment.

slides.heading: Quick check: which component?
slides.body_md: A state government in imagined Navkhand buys new ambulances for its district hospitals. Which part of aggregate demand is this?
slides.narration: Ask yourself who is doing the buying: households, firms, the government, or buyers abroad?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: aggregate demand in Navkhand
slides.body_md: Find the aggregate demand of an imagined state economy from its planned spending.
bullets: Step 1 — Add C, I and G.
Step 2 — Work out net exports: X − M.
Step 3 — Add the two results.

visual.alt: Table of planned spending in an imagined state economy, Navkhand: consumption 820, investment 260, government 180, exports 140 and imports 160 crore rupees, giving aggregate demand of 1240
visual.caption: Imagined figures. Net exports are negative here (140 − 160).

slides.narration: Consumption, investment and government spending add up to twelve hundred and sixty crore rupees. Exports are one hundred and forty and imports one hundred and sixty, so net exports are minus twenty. Adding them gives aggregate demand of twelve hundred and forty crore rupees.

slides.heading: Aggregate supply from the income side
slides.body_md: **Aggregate supply** is the total **value of output** produced. Producing output generates an equal **income**, which is either **consumed** or **saved**: **AS = C + S**.

visual.alt: Flow showing that aggregate supply is the value of output, which equals the income generated, which is either consumed or saved, so aggregate supply equals consumption plus saving
visual.caption: Aggregate supply from the income side

slides.narration: Aggregate supply is the value of everything produced in the period. Making that output creates exactly the same amount of income for the people who produced it. They either spend that income on consumption or save it. So, looked at from the income side, aggregate supply equals consumption plus saving.

slides.heading: Quick check: aggregate supply
slides.body_md: From the income side, the aggregate supply of an imagined two-sector economy can be written as…
slides.narration: What can people do with the income that production gives them?

slides.heading: Planned versus realised values
columns: **Ex ante (planned):** intentions made **before** a period, such as the investment a firm plans or the saving a family plans.
**Ex post (realised):** what **actually** happened, read from the accounts **after** the period.

visual.alt: Table comparing ex ante and ex post values: ex ante values are planned intentions made before a period by households and firms separately, and planned saving and investment may differ; ex post values are realised outcomes recorded after the period, and realised saving and investment are always equal

slides.narration: Economists use two Latin terms. Ex ante means planned: what households and firms intend at the start of a period. Ex post means realised: what actually happened, as recorded at the end. Planned saving and planned investment are made by different people, so they can differ. Realised saving and investment always turn out equal.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a hosiery cluster's investment
slides.body_md: An imagined Ludhiana hosiery cluster planned to invest ₹150 crore. A mild winter left sweaters unsold. Find its realised investment.
bullets: Step 1 — Start from planned (ex ante) investment.
Step 2 — Add the value of goods left unsold: they are added to stock.
Step 3 — The total is realised (ex post) investment.

visual.alt: Table for an imagined Ludhiana hosiery cluster: planned investment 150, unsold sweaters added to stock 25, so realised investment is 175 crore rupees
visual.caption: Imagined figures.

slides.narration: The cluster meant to invest one hundred and fifty crore rupees. Because the winter was mild, twenty-five crore rupees of sweaters stayed in the godowns. Unsold goods are added to stock, and additions to stock are investment, even though nobody planned them. So realised investment is one hundred and seventy-five crore rupees.

slides.heading: How unequal plans become equal outcomes
slides.body_md: Unplanned changes in **stock** close any gap between planned saving and planned investment.

nodes.label: Planned spending falls short of output
Unsold goods pile up as stock

visual.alt: Flow showing how a gap between planned saving and planned investment is closed: planned spending falls short of output, unsold goods pile up, the unplanned stock counts as investment so realised saving equals realised investment, and firms then cut output
visual.caption: How the plans are reconciled

slides.narration: Suppose households plan to save more than firms plan to invest. Then planned spending is less than output, and some goods are not sold. They pile up as stock, which counts as unplanned investment. Realised investment rises until it equals realised saving. Next period, firms holding unwanted stock cut their output.

slides.heading: Quick check: why the accounts balance
slides.body_md: A statistician finds that last year's realised saving and investment were exactly equal, although households had planned to save much more than firms planned to invest. Why?
slides.narration: Think about what happens to goods that are produced but not bought.

slides.heading: Effective demand
slides.body_md: **Effective demand** is the level of aggregate demand at which **AD = AS**. It decides **actual output and employment**, and it can settle **below full employment**.

visual.alt: Flow showing that where aggregate demand meets aggregate supply is effective demand, which decides actual output and employment and may be below full employment
visual.caption: Effective demand

slides.narration: Keynes used the phrase effective demand for the level of aggregate demand that actually matches aggregate supply. At that point firms sell what they produce, so it fixes output and the number of jobs. But nothing guarantees that this level is high enough to employ everyone who wants work.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: In an imagined economy of tea estates, the saving households plan for next year must always equal the investment firms plan. True or false?
slides.narration: Who makes each plan, and do they have to agree before the year starts?

slides.heading: Demand side and supply side

visual.alt: Table contrasting aggregate demand, total planned spending equal to consumption, investment, government expenditure and net exports, with aggregate supply, the total value of output, equal to consumption plus saving in two sectors

slides.narration: Keep the two sides apart. Aggregate demand is about planned spending: consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports. Aggregate supply is about output, which equals the income people earn, divided between consumption and saving. When the two are equal we have effective demand.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Planned values may differ; realised S = I always
AD = AS; fixes output, may leave unemployment

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: ex ante and ex post values, unplanned stock changes, effective demand, the components of aggregate demand, and aggregate supply as consumption plus saving

slides.narration: To sum up. Planned values can differ, but realised saving and investment are always equal, because unplanned stock changes close the gap. Effective demand is where aggregate demand equals aggregate supply. Aggregate demand is consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports; aggregate supply is consumption plus saving.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **AD = C + I + G + (X − M)** and remember **imports are subtracted**.
In two sectors write **AS = C + S** and say why: income is consumed or saved.
Define ex ante and ex post with **one example each**.
Explain equality of **realised** S and I through **unplanned stock changes**.
Effective demand: say **AD = AS** and that it **may be below full employment**.
slides.narration: State the aggregate demand formula and show that imports are taken away. Give the reason why aggregate supply equals consumption plus saving. Pair each definition of planned and realised values with a short example. When asked why realised saving equals realised investment, mention unsold stock. And never say effective demand guarantees full employment.

decks.title: Aggregate Demand, Consumption and Saving — Part 2: Propensities to Consume and Save
goals: Calculate APC and MPC from income and consumption data and explain why the MPC lies between 0 and 1
Describe the consumption function and its curve, including the break-even income
Derive a saving schedule and use APC + APS = 1 and MPC + MPS = 1 to find unknown values

slides.heading: Propensities to Consume and Save
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **consumption function**, **APC** and **MPC**, the **saving function**, **APS** and **MPS**, and two identities.

nodes.label: Average and marginal propensity to consume
Average and marginal propensity to save

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the consumption function, the average and marginal propensities to consume, the break-even income, the saving function, the average and marginal propensities to save, and the two identities
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Consumption is the largest part of aggregate demand, so we need to know how it changes with income. In this part we meet the consumption function, measure how much of income and of extra income is spent or saved, and use two simple identities to find missing values.

slides.heading: Four propensities
slides.body_md: **Average** propensities compare totals; **marginal** propensities compare **changes**.

visual.alt: Table of the four propensities: average propensity to consume is consumption over income; marginal propensity to consume is change in consumption over change in income; average propensity to save is saving over income; marginal propensity to save is change in saving over change in income

slides.narration: There are four ratios. The average propensity to consume is the share of total income spent; the marginal propensity to consume is the share of extra income spent. The average and marginal propensities to save do the same for saving. Average means total over total; marginal means change over change.

slides.heading: The consumption function
slides.body_md: **C = c̄ + bY.** In imagined Neelgiri Pradesh, **C = 90 + 0.7Y** (₹ crore): **90** is autonomous consumption and **0.7** is the MPC.

slides.narration: This curve shows planned consumption at each level of income. Even with no income, people consume ninety crore rupees, financed from past savings or loans. slides.heading: Quick check: the share of extra income spent
slides.body_md: A Kanpur shopkeeper's income rises and he spends part of the rise. The share of the extra income he spends is his…
slides.narration: Is the question about all of his income, or only the extra part?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a consumption and saving schedule
slides.body_md: Build the schedule of imagined Neelgiri Pradesh from **C = 90 + 0.7Y**.
bullets: Step 1 — C at each income from the function.
Step 2 — S = Y − C.
Step 3 — APC = C ÷ Y and APS = S ÷ Y; check they add to 1.

visual.alt: Consumption and saving schedule of imagined Neelgiri Pradesh for incomes 0 to 600 crore rupees: consumption 90, 160, 230, 300, 370, 440, 510; saving -90, -60, -30, 0, 30, 60, 90; the average propensity to consume falls from 1.6 at income 100 to 0.85 at 600
visual.caption: Imagined figures, ₹ crore. C = 90 + 0.7Y; S = Y − C.

slides.narration: Put each income into the function: at one hundred, consumption is one hundred and sixty; at six hundred, it is five hundred and ten. Saving is income minus consumption, negative below three hundred and positive above it. Dividing by income gives the average propensities, and at every income the two add up to exactly one.

slides.body_md: The **MPC stays at 0.7**; the **APC falls** as income rises, equals **1 at break-even** and stays **above the MPC**.

visual.caption: APC = 0.7 + 90 ÷ Y: always above the MPC for a straight consumption line with a positive intercept.

slides.narration: Here the two propensities are drawn against income. The marginal propensity is a flat line at zero point seven, because each extra rupee always adds seventy paise to consumption. The average propensity starts very high, falls to one at the break-even income and keeps falling towards zero point seven, without ever reaching it.

slides.heading: Quick check: where the curve meets the 45° line
slides.body_md: On a diagram of an imagined economy's consumption curve drawn with a 45° line, the point where the two meet shows the income at which…
slides.narration: Every point on the forty-five degree line has the same value on both axes. What does that mean for consumption and income?

slides.heading: Why the marginal propensity lies between 0 and 1
slides.body_md: When income rises, people **spend some** of it and **save some** of it.

visual.alt: Flow explaining why the marginal propensity to consume lies between zero and one: when income rises part of it is spent, so it is above zero, and part is saved, so it is below one
visual.caption: Why the MPC lies between 0 and 1

slides.narration: Think of what you would do with an unexpected rise in pocket money. You would spend some of it, so the marginal propensity to consume is above zero. You would probably keep some aside too, so it is below one. That is why, in the Keynesian view, it lies between zero and one.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a household's propensities
slides.body_md: Find the APC at each income and the MPC between incomes for an imagined Bhopal household.
bullets: Step 1 — APC = C ÷ Y at each income.
Step 2 — MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY between incomes.
Step 3 — Break-even where C = Y.

visual.alt: Monthly schedule of an imagined Bhopal household in thousand rupees: incomes 20, 30, 40, 50 with consumption 22, 30, 38, 46 and saving -2, 0, 2, 4; the average propensity to consume falls from 1.1 to 0.92 while the marginal propensity stays at 0.8
visual.caption: Imagined figures, ₹ thousand a month.

slides.narration: At twenty thousand rupees the family spends twenty-two thousand, so its average propensity is one point one and it dissaves. Each rise of ten thousand in income raises spending by eight thousand, so the marginal propensity is zero point eight throughout. At thirty thousand, spending equals income: the break-even point.

slides.heading: Average and marginal propensity to save
slides.body_md: **APS = S ÷ Y** (can be **negative** below break-even). **MPS = ΔS ÷ ΔY**, the slope of the saving curve.

visual.alt: Table of saving and the average propensity to save in imagined Neelgiri Pradesh: saving -60, -30, 0, 30, 60, 90 at incomes 100 to 600, so the average propensity to save rises from minus 0.6 to 0.15
visual.caption: Imagined figures, ₹ crore.

slides.narration: The average propensity to save is saving divided by income. At low incomes saving is negative, so this ratio is negative too. It rises as income grows. The marginal propensity to save is the extra saving from extra income; here it is zero point three, the slope of the saving curve.

slides.heading: The saving function
slides.body_md: **S = Y − C = −90 + 0.3Y.** It starts at **−90**, rises with slope **0.3** and crosses the income axis at **300**.

sections.heading: 1. Ex ante and ex post values
sections.body_md:
- **Ex ante (planned):** what households and firms **intend** before a period: planned consumption, saving, investment.
- **Ex post (realised):** what **actually** happened, recorded after the period.
- Planned saving (households) and planned investment (firms) are decided by **different people** for different reasons, so they **may differ**.
- Realised saving and investment are **always equal**: any gap shows up as an **unplanned change in stock**, which is counted in realised investment.
- If planned saving > planned investment: goods remain **unsold**, stocks **rise**, firms later **cut output**. If planned saving < planned investment: stocks **fall**, firms later **raise output**.

key_terms.definition_md: Planned or intended value of a variable, before the period.
Realised or actual value of a variable, after the period.
An addition to or fall in stock that firms did not intend.

sections.heading: 2. Effective demand
sections.body_md:
**Effective demand** is the level of aggregate demand at which it becomes **equal to aggregate supply**. At this level, planned spending is exactly enough to buy the output produced, so it **decides actual output and employment**.

In Keynes's view effective demand need **not** be at full employment: if planned spending is low, the economy can settle where some people who want work cannot find it (the idea of **involuntary unemployment**, taken further in the next chapter).

key_terms.definition_md: The level of aggregate demand that equals aggregate supply and so fixes output and employment.

sections.heading: 3. Aggregate demand and aggregate supply
sections.body_md:
- **Aggregate demand (AD):** total **planned** spending on final goods and services in a period.
- Open economy with government: **AD = C + I + G + (X − M)**; two sectors: AD = C + I.
- **C** households' consumption; **I** firms' investment (new capital and stock); **G** government purchases; **X − M** net exports (imports subtracted because they buy foreign output).
- **Aggregate supply (AS):** total **value of output** produced, equal to the income generated. From the income side, in two sectors, **AS = C + S**.

key_terms.definition_md: Total planned expenditure on final goods and services in an economy during a period.
Total value of goods and services produced in an economy during a period.

sections.heading: 4. The consumption function; APC and MPC
sections.body_md:
- **Consumption function:** C = f(Y); in straight-line form **C = c̄ + bY**, where **c̄** (autonomous consumption) is consumption at zero income and **b** is the MPC.
- **APC = C ÷ Y**; it can exceed 1 at low incomes (dissaving) and **falls** as income rises.
- **MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY**; normally **0 < MPC < 1** because part of extra income is saved.
- **Break-even income:** where **C = Y** (the curve meets the 45° line): S = 0 and APC = 1. For C = c̄ + bY it is **c̄ ÷ (1 − b)**; in imagined Neelgiri Pradesh, 90 ÷ 0.3 = **300**.
- For a straight-line function with c̄ > 0, **APC > MPC** at every positive income.

Consumption as a share of income, C ÷ Y.
The share of extra income spent on consumption, ΔC ÷ ΔY.
The income at which consumption equals income and saving is zero.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Adding imports in AD instead of subtracting them.
- Using totals for the MPC or changes for the APC.
- Saying the MPC can be above 1, or that the APC equals the MPC for C = c̄ + bY.
- Starting the consumption curve at the origin, or the saving curve at zero.
- Writing that ex ante saving always equals ex ante investment.
- Saying effective demand means full employment.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option, value or term.
- 2 marks: a definition with an example, or a value with working.
- 3 marks: a short schedule completed, or three linked points.
- 5 marks: parts answered in order with schedules, described diagrams and reasons.

questions.stem_md: At the start of a year, the owners of an imagined Coimbatore pump factory decide to spend ₹40 crore on new lathes. In macroeconomics this intended figure is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ex ante (planned) investment. A figure that firms or households intend or plan before the period begins is ex ante. Ex post is what actually happens by the end of the period.

questions.stem_md: When the accounts of an imagined Ranchi furniture market are closed at the end of the year, the investment actually recorded there is its
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ex post investment. Investment measured after the period, as it actually turned out, is ex post (realised) investment. Planned figures are ex ante.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Ludhiana hosiery cluster planned investment of ₹150 crore, but weak winter sales left an extra ₹25 crore of unsold sweaters in its godowns. Its ex post investment is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹175 crore. Unsold goods added to stock count as (unplanned) investment, so realised investment = planned 150 + unplanned 25 = 175.

questions.stem_md: In the Keynesian sense, effective demand in an imagined economy of small towns along the Konkan coast is the level of aggregate demand that

options.text_md: exceeds aggregate supply at full employment
equals aggregate supply, so it decides the actual level of output and employment
is planned by the government in its budget

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** equals aggregate supply, so it decides the actual level of output and employment. Effective demand is the point where aggregate demand equals aggregate supply; that level of demand is actually realised and fixes output and employment. It need not be at full employment.

questions.stem_md: A statistician studying an imagined economy finds that in last year's final accounts saving and investment were exactly equal, even though households had planned to save far more than firms planned to invest. This is best explained by the fact that

options.text_md: planned (ex ante) saving and investment are always equal
the government forced firms to invest more
realised (ex post) saving and investment are always equal because unplanned stock changes absorb the gap
households must have spent all their income

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** realised (ex post) saving and investment are always equal because unplanned stock changes absorb the gap. Ex post, saving and investment are always equal: the excess saving shows up as unsold goods, which raise realised investment by the same amount. Ex ante they can differ.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In an imagined island economy, realised saving and realised investment for last year turn out equal although planned saving exceeded planned investment.

**Reason (R):** Goods that were produced but not sold are added to stocks and counted as unplanned investment.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: the shortfall in planned spending leaves unsold output, and this unplanned addition to stock raises realised investment until it equals realised saving.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In an imagined economy of tea estates, the saving that households plan for next year must always equal the investment that firms plan for next year.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Planned (ex ante) saving and investment are made by different people for different reasons, so they can differ. Only realised (ex post) saving and investment are always equal.

questions.stem_md: The level of aggregate demand at which it becomes equal to aggregate supply is called ___ demand.
questions.solution_md: That level of aggregate demand is called effective demand, because it is actually realised in output and employment.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between ex ante and ex post consumption, using the shopping of an imagined Guwahati family as your example.
questions.solution_md: Planned versus realised, each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Ex ante** consumption is what the family **plans** to spend, say ₹30,000 for the coming month. **Ex post** consumption is what it **actually** spent once the month is over, say ₹33,000 after an unexpected wedding gift.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by effective demand? Why does an imagined district of handloom villages not automatically produce at full employment?
questions.solution_md: Meaning, then the link to employment.

answer.model_answer_md: **Effective demand** is the level of aggregate demand that **equals aggregate supply**; it fixes actual output and jobs. Since it is set by **what buyers plan to spend**, it can settle **below** the full-employment output, leaving some weavers without work.

questions.stem_md: The hosiery cluster in imagined Ludhiana planned investment of ₹150 crore for the year, but ₹25 crore of sweaters stayed unsold. (a) Find realised investment. (b) Explain why unsold goods count as investment, and what the cluster is likely to do next year.
questions.solution_md: Planned plus unplanned investment; firms respond by cutting output.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Realised investment = 150 + 25 = **₹175 crore**.
(b) Investment includes **additions to stock**; unsold sweaters are goods produced but not consumed, so they add to **inventory**. Because this stock was **not planned**, firms are likely to **cut production** next year.

marking_scheme.step: Unsold goods are additions to stock

questions.stem_md: Explain why planned saving and planned investment in an imagined economy can be unequal, while realised saving and realised investment are always equal.
questions.solution_md: Different deciders, then unplanned stock changes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Planned** saving is decided by **households** (income, thrift), planned investment by **firms** (expected profit, interest), so the two plans need not match.
2. If planned saving exceeds planned investment, **some output is not bought** and piles up as **stock**.
3. This **unplanned stock** counts as investment, so **realised** investment rises to equal realised saving.

marking_scheme.step: Mismatch shows up as stock change
Unplanned stock makes realised values equal

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about an imagined economy of small towns in Bundelkhand. [2 + 3]

(a) Distinguish between ex ante and ex post saving, with an example of each.
(b) Suppose households there plan to save ₹50 crore but firms plan to invest only ₹40 crore. Explain what happens to stocks, why realised saving and investment are still equal, and how firms are likely to react.
questions.solution_md: Definitions, then the stock adjustment and the firms' response.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Ex ante saving** is the saving households **plan** at the start of a period (₹50 crore in the case). **Ex post saving** is what they **actually** saved at its end.
(b) Planned spending falls short of output by **₹10 crore**, so goods worth ₹10 crore **remain unsold** and **stocks rise**. This **unplanned inventory** counts as investment, so realised investment becomes 40 + 10 = **₹50 crore**, equal to realised saving. Firms find stocks piling up, so they **cut output and employment** in the next period.

questions.stem_md: Aggregate demand in an imagined open economy with a government means the total

options.text_md: planned spending on final goods and services in the economy during a period
value of goods actually produced during a period
income earned by the factors of production

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** planned spending on final goods and services in the economy during a period. Aggregate demand is total planned (ex ante) expenditure on final goods and services. The value of output produced is aggregate supply.

questions.stem_md: Which expression gives aggregate demand in an imagined economy that trades with other countries and has a government?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** C + I + G + (X − M). AD adds household consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports (exports minus imports).

questions.stem_md: From the income side, aggregate supply of an imagined two-sector economy can be written as

options.text_md: C + I, because output is either consumed or invested
C + S, because income is either consumed or saved
S + I, because both are equal ex post
C − S, because saving is a leakage

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** C + S, because income is either consumed or saved. Aggregate supply is the value of output, which equals the income generated; income is either consumed or saved, so AS = C + S.

questions.stem_md: Families in an imagined economy start buying more imported smartphones and fewer phones assembled at home, while their total spending stays the same. Aggregate demand for that economy's output will

options.text_md: fall, because imports are subtracted from spending
rise, because total spending is unchanged
stay the same, because imports are part of consumption
rise, because imports add to the government's customs revenue

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** fall, because imports are subtracted from spending. Spending on imports goes to output produced abroad, so it is subtracted in AD = C + I + G + (X − M). A switch towards imports lowers AD for domestic output.

questions.stem_md: A state government in imagined Navkhand buys new ambulances for its district hospitals. In aggregate demand this purchase is part of
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** government expenditure (G). Purchases of goods and services by the government are government expenditure, the G component of AD.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If an imagined economy's imports exceed its exports, the net-exports component of its aggregate demand is negative.

**Reason (R):** Imports add to the demand for goods produced within the economy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: X − M < 0 when M > X. R is false: imports are spending on goods produced abroad, so they reduce demand for domestic output, which is why they are subtracted.

questions.stem_md: Since income is either consumed or saved, aggregate supply in a two-sector economy can be written as C + ___.
questions.solution_md: Aggregate supply = C + S: consumption plus saving.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined state economy of Navkhand (₹ crore), planned consumption is 820, planned investment 260, government purchases 180, exports 140 and imports 160. Find its aggregate demand (in ₹ crore).
Match each spending decision in an imagined coastal economy with the component of aggregate demand it belongs to.

options.text_md: A fishing family buys a new refrigerator
A seafood exporter builds a cold-storage plant
The state builds a new fish-landing jetty
A hotel chain abroad buys frozen prawns from the coast

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Household purchases are C; new plant by firms is I; public works are G; sales to buyers abroad are X.

questions.stem_md: Name the four components of aggregate demand in an open economy with a government, giving one imagined Indian example of any two.
questions.solution_md: All four components; any two examples.

answer.model_answer_md: **C** (household consumption), **I** (investment), **G** (government expenditure) and **(X − M)** (net exports). Examples: a Jaipur family buying a scooter is **C**; a Pune firm installing a new robot arm is **I**.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between aggregate demand and aggregate supply for an imagined district economy.
questions.solution_md: Spending side versus output/income side.

answer.model_answer_md: **Aggregate demand** is the total **planned spending** on final goods and services (C + I + G + X − M). **Aggregate supply** is the total **value of output** produced, which equals the **income** generated (C + S in two sectors).

questions.stem_md: In imagined Navkhand (₹ crore), C = 820, I = 260, G = 180, X = 140 and M = 160. (a) Calculate aggregate demand. (b) If imports rise by 40 while everything else stays the same, find the new aggregate demand and explain the change.
questions.solution_md: AD formula, then the effect of higher imports.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) AD = 820 + 260 + 180 + (140 − 160) = **1240**.
(b) Net exports fall to 140 − 200 = -60, so AD = **1200**. More of the spending now goes to **goods produced abroad**, so demand for **Navkhand's own output falls** by 40.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: imports leak out of domestic demand

questions.stem_md: Explain why each of the following is treated as it is in measuring the aggregate demand of an imagined economy: (a) investment by firms, (b) government purchases, (c) imports.
questions.solution_md: Each component with the reason for its sign.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) **Investment** is spending on **new capital goods and stocks**, so it is **added**. (b) **Government purchases** of goods and services also buy current output, so they are **added**. (c) **Imports** are spending on output **produced abroad**; they are already inside C, I and G, so they are **subtracted**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the imagined state economy of Navkhand (₹ crore): C = 820, I = 260, G = 180, X = 140, M = 160. [3 + 2]

(a) Explain the components of aggregate demand and calculate Navkhand's aggregate demand.
(b) If the value of output (aggregate supply) this year is ₹1,300 crore, state what will happen to unplanned stocks, and why.
questions.solution_md: Components and AD, then AS above AD.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Aggregate demand is the total **planned spending** on the final output of Navkhand. **C** is households' spending on consumer goods and services; **I** is firms' spending on new machines, buildings and additions to stock; **G** is the government's purchases of goods and services; **X − M** is exports minus imports, since imports buy output made outside Navkhand. AD = 820 + 260 + 180 + (140 − 160) = **₹1,240 crore**; net exports are negative (−20).
(b) Output of ₹1,300 crore exceeds planned spending of ₹1,240 crore by **₹60 crore**. Goods worth 60 therefore remain **unsold** and **unplanned stocks rise** by 60, which raises realised investment above planned investment. Holding unwanted stock, firms are likely to **reduce output and employment** in the next period.

questions.stem_md: For an imagined Bhopal household, the average propensity to consume is

options.text_md: the change in consumption divided by the change in income

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** consumption divided by income. APC = C ÷ Y, the share of income that is consumed. ΔC ÷ ΔY is the MPC; S ÷ Y is the APS.

questions.stem_md: A Kanpur shopkeeper's monthly income rises and he spends part of the rise. The share of the extra income that he spends is his
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** marginal propensity to consume. MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY: the fraction of additional income spent on consumption.

questions.stem_md: In the Keynesian consumption function, the MPC of an imagined economy normally lies
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** between 0 and 1. When income rises, people spend some of the increase but not all of it, so 0 < MPC < 1.

questions.stem_md: In the consumption function C = 90 + 0.7Y of imagined Neelgiri Pradesh (₹ crore), the term 90 shows

options.text_md: consumption even when income is zero, financed from past savings or borrowing
the saving of households at zero income

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** consumption even when income is zero, financed from past savings or borrowing. The constant 90 is autonomous consumption: what people must consume even at zero income. 0.7 is the MPC; saving at zero income is −90.

questions.stem_md: In the Bhopal household's schedule (₹ thousand), consumption is 22 when income is 20. Its APC at this income is above 1, which means the family is

options.text_md: saving a large part of its income
dissaving: spending more than its income from past savings or loans

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** dissaving: spending more than its income from past savings or loans. APC = 22 ÷ 20 = 1.1 > 1: consumption exceeds income, so saving is -2 (dissaving). The MPC is still 0.8.

questions.stem_md: For Neelgiri Pradesh with C = 90 + 0.7Y, what happens to the APC as income rises from 100 to 600?

options.text_md: It falls from 1.6 towards 0.7 but always stays above the MPC
It falls below 0.7 at high incomes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It falls from 1.6 towards 0.7 but always stays above the MPC. APC = 90 ÷ Y + 0.7: 1.6 at 100 and 0.85 at 600. As Y grows, 90 ÷ Y shrinks, so APC falls towards 0.7 but never reaches it.

questions.stem_md: On a diagram of an imagined economy's consumption curve drawn with a 45° line, the point where the two meet shows the income at which

options.text_md: consumption equals income and saving is zero

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** consumption equals income and saving is zero. Every point on the 45° line has C = Y. Where the consumption curve meets it, C = Y and S = 0: the break-even point.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When the income of households in an imagined economy rises by ₹100 crore, their consumption rises by less than ₹100 crore.

**Reason (R):** People usually save a part of any increase in their income.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: because part of the extra income is saved, consumption rises by less than income, so MPC < 1.

questions.stem_md: True or false? For the linear consumption function C = 90 + 0.7Y of imagined Neelgiri Pradesh, the APC is greater than the MPC at every positive income.
questions.solution_md: **True.** APC = 0.7 + 90 ÷ Y, and 90 ÷ Y > 0 for every positive income, so APC > MPC = 0.7.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Mangaluru cashew-processing family earns ₹800 hundred a month and spends ₹680 hundred. Calculate its average propensity to consume.
When the income of an imagined Nashik grape-growers' cooperative rises from ₹500 lakh to ₹700 lakh, its members' consumption rises from ₹420 lakh to ₹570 lakh. Find the MPC.
In an imagined hill economy, autonomous consumption is ₹30 crore and the MPC is 0.6. Find consumption when income is ₹250 crore (in ₹ crore).
For the Sundarban fishing village (₹ lakh) with consumption 120, 200, 270, 330 at incomes 100, 200, 300, 400, arrange the incomes from the HIGHEST to the LOWEST average propensity to consume.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). APC = C ÷ Y: 1.2, 1, 0.9, 0.825, which falls as income rises.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between APC and MPC, using the figures of an imagined Bhopal household whose monthly consumption rises from ₹30 thousand to ₹38 thousand when income rises from ₹30 thousand to ₹40 thousand.
questions.solution_md: Each ratio defined and worked out.

answer.model_answer_md: **APC** = C ÷ Y, the share of income consumed: at income 40 it is 38 ÷ 40 = **0.95**. **MPC** = ΔC ÷ ΔY, the share of extra income consumed: 8 ÷ 10 = **0.8**.

questions.stem_md: Why does the MPC of households in an imagined district town lie between zero and one? Give two reasons.
questions.solution_md: Some spent, some saved.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. When income rises people **spend some** of the increase, so MPC is **above zero**.
2. They also **save some** of it for the future, so consumption rises by **less than** income and MPC is **below one**.

questions.stem_md:
The table shows the monthly income and consumption of an imagined Bhopal household (₹ thousand).

| Income (₹ thousand) | Consumption (₹ thousand) |
|---|---|
| 20 | 22 |
| 30 | 30 |
| 40 | 38 |
| 50 | 46 |

Calculate the APC at each income and the MPC between successive incomes, and state the break-even income.
questions.solution_md: APC = C ÷ Y; MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY; break-even where C = Y.

answer.model_answer_md: **APC = C ÷ Y** at each income: 22 ÷ 20, 30 ÷ 30, 38 ÷ 40 and 46 ÷ 50, giving **1.1, 1, 0.95, 0.92**. **MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY**: consumption rises by 8 for every rise of 10 in income, so the MPC is **0.8, 0.8, 0.8**. The **break-even income is ₹30 thousand**, where consumption equals income (30 = 30), saving is zero and APC = 1; below it the family dissaves.

questions.stem_md:
Study the income and consumption of an imagined Sundarban fishing village.

| Income (₹ lakh) | Consumption (₹ lakh) |
|---|---|
| 100 | 120 |
| 200 | 200 |
| 300 | 270 |
| 400 | 330 |

Calculate the MPC between successive incomes and comment on what the trend suggests about how the villagers use extra income.
questions.solution_md: MPC values, then interpretation.

answer.model_answer_md: **MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY:** 80 ÷ 100, 70 ÷ 100 and 60 ÷ 100, that is **0.8, 0.7, 0.6**. The MPC **falls as income rises**. At low incomes almost every extra rupee goes on **necessities** such as food and boat repairs, but as families become better off they **save a larger share** of each extra rupee, so consumption rises by less and less.

questions.stem_md: Describe the consumption curve of imagined Neelgiri Pradesh, C = 90 + 0.7Y, drawn with a 45° line, and identify three of its features.
questions.solution_md: Intercept, slope, break-even point.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It starts at **90 on the vertical axis** (autonomous consumption), not at the origin.
2. It slopes upward with **slope 0.7 (the MPC)**, flatter than the 45° line.
3. It cuts the 45° line at the **break-even income of 300**: to the left C > Y (dissaving), to the right C < Y (saving).

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about imagined Neelgiri Pradesh, where C = 90 + 0.7Y (₹ crore). [3 + 2]

(a) Prepare a consumption and saving schedule for incomes 0, 200, 400 and 600, and find the APC and APS at 400 and 600.
(b) Find the break-even income and explain what it shows.
questions.solution_md: Schedule from the function, ratios, then C = Y.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Putting each income into the function gives **C:** 90, 230, 370, 510 at incomes 0, 200, 400 and 600. Saving is income minus consumption, **S = Y − C:** -90, -30, 30, 90. At 400, APC = 370 ÷ 400 = **0.925** and APS = 30 ÷ 400 = **0.075**; at 600, APC = 510 ÷ 600 = **0.85** and APS = 90 ÷ 600 = **0.15**. In each case APC + APS = 1.

|---|---|
| 100 | 120 |

questions.solution_md: Ratios, then a reasoned judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **APC = C ÷ Y:** 120 ÷ 100, 200 ÷ 200, 270 ÷ 300 and 330 ÷ 400, giving **1.2, 1, 0.9, 0.825**. **MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY:** consumption rises by 80, 70 and 60 for each rise of 100 in income, so the MPC is **0.8, 0.7, 0.6**.

The MPC **falls to 0.7 and then 0.6** at higher incomes, so the village spends a **smaller share** of each extra rupee as it becomes richer and saves the rest. A government that wants to raise spending should note that extra income given to **poorer** households raises consumption **more** than the same amount given to better-off ones.

(ii) Explain which household saves the larger share of its income now, and which would add more to consumption out of a further rise in income.
questions.solution_md: APC and MPC, then compare APS and MPC.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Sinhas: **APC = 36,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.9** and **MPC = 6,000 ÷ 10,000 = 0.6**. Ansaris: **APC = 30,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.75** and **MPC = 7,000 ÷ 10,000 = 0.7**.
(ii) The **Ansaris** save the larger share of their present income: their **APS is 0.25**, against 0.1 for the Sinhas. But the Ansaris also have the **higher MPC (0.7)**, so out of a further rise in income they would add **more to consumption** than the Sinhas. A high average saving rate does not mean a low marginal one.

questions.stem_md:
In the imagined state economy of Navkhand (₹ crore), planned spending is C = 820, I = 260, G = 180, X = 140 and M = 160, while firms produce output worth ₹1,200 crore. [2 + 2]

(i) Calculate aggregate demand and compare it with output.
(ii) Explain what happens to stocks and to ex post investment, and how firms are likely to respond.
questions.solution_md: AD versus output, then the stock adjustment.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) AD = C + I + G + (X − M) = 820 + 260 + 180 + (140 − 160) = **1240**. This planned spending **exceeds output of 1,200 by 40**, so there is excess demand.
(ii) Buyers want more than is being produced, so firms meet the extra demand by **selling from their stocks**. Stocks **fall by 40**, an unplanned fall in inventory, so ex post investment is **40 less** than planned investment. Seeing their stocks run down, firms are likely to **raise output and employment** in the next period.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Stocks fall; ex post investment below plan

(ii) Find saving and the APS at an income of ₹500 crore.
questions.solution_md: Saving function, S = 0, then S and APS at 500.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Saving is income minus consumption: S = Y − C = Y − (60 + 0.8Y) = **−60 + 0.2Y**, so the MPS is 0.2. The break-even income is where saving is zero: 0.2Y = 60, so Y = 60 ÷ 0.2 = **300**. At this income consumption also equals income (60 + 0.8 × 300 = 300).
(ii) At an income of 500, S = −60 + 0.2 × 500 = −60 + 100 = **40**. The APS is saving divided by income: **APS = 40 ÷ 500 = 0.08**, so the APC is 0.92.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about an imagined economy where households plan to save ₹120 crore and firms plan to invest ₹100 crore. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain the meaning of ex ante and ex post saving and investment, and show how the two plans are brought to equality ex post.
(ii) "Effective demand always ensures full employment." Evaluate this statement using the idea of aggregate demand and aggregate supply.
questions.solution_md: Ex ante/ex post with the stock adjustment; then evaluate.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Ex ante** values are **planned** at the start of the period; **ex post** values are **realised** at its end. Here planned saving exceeds planned investment by **₹20 crore**, so spending on output falls short by 20 and goods worth **20 remain unsold**. These add to **stocks** as **unplanned investment**, so realised investment = 100 + 20 = **120**, equal to realised saving.
(ii) The statement is **not correct**. **Effective demand** is the level of aggregate demand at which it **equals aggregate supply**; it fixes actual output and employment. But it depends on **planned spending**, which may be **too low** to buy the output of a fully employed workforce. The economy can then settle at an equilibrium with **involuntary unemployment**. Full employment is only **one possible** position of effective demand.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Meanings of ex ante and ex post
